output.headline: NHS England says it balanced its books for first time in a decade
output.bodyHtml:
NHS England did not respond directly to a request for comment over widespread cost-cutting across the health service, but a spokesperson said it 'did an amazing job last year to bring its finances in within budget for the first time in more than a decade, while also delivering record levels of treatments and operations to patients'.

The spokesperson said NHS boards 'are rightly being transparent about financial risks and taking action to mitigate them', with organisations across the NHS 'working hard to improve productivity, live within their means and make the best use of taxpayers' money, while continuing to deliver the care people need'.

Dozens of hospitals are nonetheless so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make 'unpalatable' cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.

Twenty-seven of those trusts are in such dire financial straits that they have rated lack of money as the biggest threat they face. Six have given that danger a rating of 25 – the highest possible score – in their risk register. A much-larger number of trusts have launched cost-cutting programmes to save as much as £106m each this year by limiting the services they provide and shrinking their workforces, despite understaffing being widespread across the NHS.

The six include King’s College hospital NHS trust in London, which is seeking to save £85m this year, and the St George’s, Epsom and St Helier hospital group, also in the capital, which has a savings target of £91m. The others are the North Midlands, Gloucestershire, and Doncaster and Bassetlaw acute trusts, and Birmingham and Solihull mental health trust.

Trust bosses say their finances are in a 'precarious' and 'severe' state. They blame rising drug prices, strikes and the cost of covering pay rises, the extra demand caused by this summer’s heatwaves, and the introduction of electronic health records. Privately they accuse NHS England of forcing them to adopt unreasonable savings targets in order to help the health service as a whole balance its books, because hospitals have been told to stop overspending.

In an illustration of the impact that savings drives can have, in August people in Kent with cancer had to wait up to a month for appointments before they could start chemotherapy; this was because the cancer unit had fewer nurses on duty than usual after the East Kent trust cut rates of pay to work extra 'bank' shifts as part of a cost-cutting plan, which led to understaffing.

The trust admitted in a paper, which its board discussed, that it was seeing 'increasing waits for new patient appointments and pre-chemo appointments … due to lack of take-up of bank shifts due to [pay] rate changes'.

In September, York and Scarborough trust said it would shut a 28-bed ward at Bridlington community hospital, a 'step-down' facility that looks after people recently discharged from hospital before they go home, to help it save £1m. It did so despite the risk this will add to pressures on beds at its two acute hospitals.

The trust also looked into withdrawing the maternity and radiology services it provided at Whitby community hospital as another of its 'opportunities for efficiencies', to save an estimated £200,000. However, those plans were 'no longer being considered', it said. It is also considering cutting the opening hours of the three urgent treatment centres it runs in York, Scarborough and Malton, to save a further £200,000, even though such services are intended to prevent overcrowding of A&E units. The trust refused to answer questions the Guardian asked about that.

Harrogate and district trust has decided to stop providing out-of-hours GP care in Hambleton and Richmond, covering a large swathe of rural North Yorkshire, after 15 years because it can no longer afford to do so. It is unclear who will offer patients that service in the future.

Sherwood Forest trust’s plan to close a hydrotherapy pool at King’s Mill hospital in Sutton-in-Ashfield, to save £150,000 to £200,000, has provoked an outcry. The pool is used to help rehabilitate about 1,500 patients a year, including those with long-term health conditions or those recovering from car crashes or a hip replacement, said the local Labour MP, Steve Yemm.

Sara Hazzard, of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy, said: 'The proposed closing of this pool is deeply concerning and risks depriving vulnerable patients of vital specialist rehabilitation. For people with chronic long-term conditions, aquatic physiotherapy is a clinical lifeline. The warmth and buoyancy of the water help people to manage pain, exercise and maintain mobility when land-based rehabilitation may not be suitable.'

Sherwood Forest also recently admitted in a paper discussed by its board that 'financial restraints, including the need to reduce bank and agency spend, may lead to impacts on ability to maintain patient care and safety'.

Torbay and South Devon trust is axing 199 non-clinical posts and charging staff more for parking and food to help it meet its £54.4m 'cost improvement plan' target. It has an underlying deficit of £100m.

In a paper submitted to its 5 November board meeting, it said it would 'assess all available options to close the forecast risk gap and deliver financial plan, including "unpalatable" and high-risk options'. NHS England has told its leaders to break even this year or risk having their performance being reviewed, which could lead to them being replaced.

The NHS is so short of cash that it cannot afford to have the number of beds it needs to help hospitals cope this winter, Emma Rowland, NHS England’s executive director for performance and recovery, told MPs earlier this month.

One trust boss said: 'I have been a [trust] chief executive for more than 10 years and the NHS’s finances are as tough as they have ever been. Many trusts are forecasting deficits larger than recent years. Balancing the books often means breakeven. Very few trusts will break even and many will miss their financial plan for this year.'

Trusts are also cutting jobs in a desperate effort to save money. For example, Nottingham university hospitals trust plans to shrink its workforce by 1,279 to help it meet its £106m savings target for 2026-27. It admits that a third of its identified savings are 'high risk'.

Similarly, Barts health trust in London aims to axe 1,100 posts to save money.

Dr Tony O’Sullivan, a co-chair of the campaign group Keep Our NHS Public, said: 'This financial straitjacket on the NHS is deeply irresponsible and the consequences are devastating. Years of underinvestment have left trusts being asked to make huge savings while demand and costs keep rising.

'AI can’t staff a ward, and another reorganisation won’t reopen a single bed. Closing step-down beds means some patients will spend longer in hospital waiting for somewhere safe to go. That leaves fewer beds for people waiting in A&E and makes it harder to carry out planned operations.'

O’Sullivan added that Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, should ask the chancellor for emergency funding for the NHS to help it cope with the pressure it is under. The Department of Health and Social Care’s total spending for 2025-26 was £217bn, most of which went to the NHS.
output.standfirst: NHS England says it balanced its books for the first time in a decade while delivering record care, but 31 trusts now say drastic savings demands risk 'unpalatable' cuts to staff and services.
output.progress: NHS England says boards are being transparent about financial risks and taking action to improve productivity and live within their means.

output.headline: Crews rescued after drone strikes hit two Russia-linked ships
output.bodyHtml:
Rescuers reached everyone aboard two Russia-linked ships hit by suspected Ukrainian sea-drone strikes over the weekend, officials in Libya and Finland said, after the attacks sank a Russian warship in the Mediterranean and set a cargo vessel ablaze in the Baltic.

Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the crew of the Ascalon, a Russia-linked cargo ship hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi hours after the warship strike. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries; the number of injured and their nationalities are not known.

Initial reports said several drones were launched at the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped in Benghazi to refuel and take on supplies; at least four were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering a dramatic night-time explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.

Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.

Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.

“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
output.standfirst: Crews were rescued or evacuated from two Russia-linked ships hit by suspected Ukrainian sea-drone strikes, which sank a warship off Benghazi and set a cargo vessel ablaze in the Baltic, extending the war far beyond the frontline; the UN has urged an independent investigation.
output.progress: Libyan naval forces rescued the crew of the Ascalon cargo ship off Benghazi, and the UN mission in Libya has called for an independent investigation into the attacks.

output.headline: Coalition of nations stands firm against a fossil-fuel-silent climate deal at Cop31
output.bodyHtml:
The EU, the UK and a coalition of mostly poorer and climate-vulnerable nations refused on Sunday to accept a Cop31 deal they said failed to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the longest UN climate summit ever.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.

But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.

“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.

But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”

Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.

Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.

But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”
output.standfirst: A coalition of mostly poorer and climate-vulnerable nations, together with the EU and UK, refused to accept Cop31's 'Antalya pact' because it failed to mention fossil fuels, leaving the summit without an overarching agreement.
output.progress: Simon Stiell, the UN climate chief, says a number of agenda items still passed with 'real progress and concrete results'.

output.headline: Oxfam report maps scale of toxic contamination left across Gaza
output.bodyHtml:
Israel’s assault on Gaza has left a severe environmental legacy, according to a report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs): poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air now threaten the life-support systems the population depends on for survival, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.

Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”

He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”

In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.

Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.

Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.

Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.

“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”

He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.

The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.

The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.

“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”

Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.

“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.

The Israeli government has been contacted for comment.
output.standfirst: The report, by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory, finds poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threaten Gaza's population for generations, after an assault that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.

output.headline: Police reflect on 'areas of learning' after Lewis-Ranwell killings failures
output.bodyHtml:
A police spokesperson said Devon and Cornwall police were addressing 'areas of learning' and would reflect on the recommendations of the inquest jury, adding: 'Our thoughts, as always, remain with the loved ones of Anthony Payne and Dick and Roger Carter.'

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Officers were found to have ignored warnings from a national database as well as a mental health assessor, according to a joint investigation by the Sunday Times and BBC Radio 4’s File On 4 Investigates.

Numerous failings were found in hours of police video, detention logs and witness testimony. The medical professional who was sent to examine Lewis-Ranwell, 27, did not have expertise in mental health and dismissed his unpredictable behaviour.

There were also failures to record and share key details that would have built up a picture of the severity of Lewis-Ranwell’s mental illness.

Officers did not know that by law they had the power to detain him under the Mental Health Act without a medical assessment. Warnings from Lewis-Ranwell’s mother, that he was having a psychotic episode and should be kept in custody, were also ignored.

The families of the three men have called on the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to open an investigation into Devon and Cornwall police, but they are still waiting for answers and an apology.

The watchdog has said that the force should investigate itself, but they have heard nothing for two years.

Two days before the murders took place, Lewis-Ranwell was arrested after breaking into a farm. After his release he was arrested a second time for attacking a farmer with a 1.2-metre (4ft) logging saw.

Despite exhibiting disturbing behaviour in custody – police bodycam footage shows him semi-naked, hissing, spitting and punching at the hatch window to his cell, while ranting about paedophiles and seeing animals – he was released again.

Following a rampage that lasted hours and in which he threatened multiple people, he killed the three men, bludgeoning Payne with a hammer and killing the twins with a spade.

A trial at Exeter crown court in December 2019 found Lewis-Ranwell not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a hospital restriction order, where he will stay until agencies are confident he could be released back into the community.

One psychiatrist who studied the case told the court he believed Lewis-Ranwell, a former public schoolboy from Croyde, north Devon, was “one of the illest people” he had come across.

Last month an inquest found failings by police led to his release after a doctor missed “clear signs of delusion and disordered thinking”.

Amanda Taylor told the Sunday Times that her family was still seeking justice for her uncles the Carter brothers and that they want the IOPC to revisit the case.

“All I want is for just one of the agencies involved to stand up and say: ‘We are so sorry. Serious mistakes were made. We recognise the devastating consequences of those failures and we will do everything in our power to make sure this never happens again,’” she said.

Lewis-Ranwell’s case is one of several where failures from the police and mental health services to manage risk have resulted in tragedy.

A review by the Care Quality Commission of the treatment of Valdo Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia and killed three people in Nottingham in 2023, concluded that a “series of errors and misjudgments” led to him being discharged, despite repeatedly not taking medication and showing signs of aggression.

The report concluded that there are “systemic issues with community mental health care which, without immediate action, will continue to pose an inherent risk to patient and public safety”.

NHS England has since strengthened guidance around community mental health support for people with severe mental illnesses who face high risk or struggle to engage with services.

Noting that there are an estimated 100 to 120 mental health-related killings in the UK every year, Julian Hendy, of the victims’ charity Hundred Families, said: “In my view, had the lessons in the Lewis-Ranwell case been learnt earlier, and effective action taken, there is a real chance that the Nottingham attacks could well have been prevented. Services aren’t learning and totally innocent people are losing their lives as a result.”

The IOPC said the family had a right to ask for a review of the internal investigation and that it had not yet received a request.
output.standfirst: Devon and Cornwall police say they are addressing 'areas of learning' and reflecting on inquest recommendations, after a catalogue of failures preceded Alexander Lewis-Ranwell's release before he killed three people in Exeter in 2019.
output.progress: Devon and Cornwall police say they are addressing 'areas of learning' and reflecting on the inquest jury's recommendations.

output.headline: Pip review, shaped by disabled people, recommends overhaul for all ages
output.bodyHtml:
A long-awaited review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system, shaped with the input of disability rights advocates, will this week recommend that it is overhauled and retained for people of all ages, a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped for under-25s.

The final report on Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister.

Its conclusions are understood to be very similar to a draft set of recommendations that emerged in September, which called for a series of changes, particularly to the system of assessment, to take better account of conditions that vary over time.

This would involve significant changes to Pip, which is intended to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability. An interim report by Timms’ committee described the benefit as widely valued but “no longer fit for purpose”.

However, it would retain the system for all ages, while last week’s report by Alan Milburn on worklessness among young people called for it to be scrapped for adults under 25 and replaced by an “additional cost allowance”, part of a wider network of job-based help for this age group.

Government officials have pushed back on the idea of a clash, saying Milburn’s review was commissioned after the Timms process had begun, and that about 90% of the Pip caseload involves people over 25.

But with Timms’ recommendations understood to be quite broad, Burnham and his ministers will need to make a series of decisions about what comes next, on a deeply sensitive subject. Keir Starmer was forced to abandon planned changes in 2025 after a rebellion by Labour MPs.

Related: Age instead of need drives Alan Milburn’s new reforms. Welcome to the two-tier welfare state | Frances Ryan

There was widespread shock among disability campaigners and charities at the Milburn report’s recommendations to scrap Pip and universal credit health benefit payments for under-25s as part of efforts to boost jobs and training for young people not in education, employment or training.

The review steering group is co-chaired by Timms and the disability rights advocates Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan, and most of its 12 members have lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions.

There are reportedly worries among some members of the Timms review board over the scale of Milburn’s proposals on Pip, which would cut £3.6bn from spending on young people. “Some members are really concerned,” one source told the Guardian.

The report will include short-term overhauls, within the current spending round, and longer-term ones. Many of the specifics for the latter would need to be decided by ministers before they legislate next year.

Burnham faces pressure from the Conservatives to reduce the overall cost of working-age benefits. He has said this is his plan but he has pushed back against the idea of what he called “crude cuts”, saying these often just created costs elsewhere.

The Timms review, framed by ministers as a groundbreaking “co-produced” policy initiative, was seen as an attempt to restore trust among disabled people after the collapse of the Pip plans under Starmer, which were based on £5bn in cuts.

The interim report in July and further emerging findings in September confirmed a consensus view that Pip was unfit for purpose and that a major overhaul was needed to make the benefit fair, humane and efficient.

It raised the prospect that some claimants could in future receive “in kind” awards such as services, aid or training alongside basic cash awards.

But it underlined that cash payments were “the foundation” of a future reformed disability benefit, that it would not be means-tested and that any “reformed benefit will be designed with disabled people and those with long-term health conditions, and tested to make sure it works before it is rolled out”. There was no mention of scrapping Pip for under-25s or any other age groups.

Until recently, most disability charities had been optimistic that the Timms review – the remit of which did not include the costs of Pip or potential cuts in spending – would lead to much-needed changes and improve the lives of the 4 million adults who claim it.

But the timing and scope of the Milburn review, which has been conspicuously welcomed by ministers, has dented that confidence.

A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “The Timms review interim report made clear that Pip is no longer fit for purpose. When the final report is published, we will consider the recommendations alongside the Milburn review.”
output.standfirst: The final report, led by minister Stephen Timms with disabled people's input, would retain Pip for everyone, in contrast to last week's Milburn review, which called for the benefit to be scrapped for under-25s.
output.progress: Stephen Timms' review, co-produced with disability rights advocates, aims to make Pip fair, humane and workable for claimants.

output.headline: Burnham presses tech firms to remove Russell Brand's prison messages
output.bodyHtml:
Russell Brand’s wife, Laura, has promised to 'absolutely honour' rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.

On Thursday night, Burnham said he 'wouldn’t leap' to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: 'I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.'

This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Russell Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.

Laura Brand began the latest episode of Sunday Service – described as a Christian series, which the couple started together six months ago – by telling viewers: 'Last week’s episode drew considerable amount of attention and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that.'

She went on to address scrutiny regarding her continuing to run her husband’s YouTube channel, amid a Ministry of Justice inquiry focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent 'serious distress' to the victims of crime.

'I am choosing to continue Sunday Service because I really enjoy it,' she said. 'It is also a place where I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media’s image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny.'

In the previous episode, the first published since Brand was jailed – after being convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November – Laura Brand read out a message from him protesting that he was not guilty.

The video, titled 'The Good Work Continues', has remained on YouTube despite ministers repeatedly asking for it to be removed.

That video has now accumulated more than 1m views, becoming the best-performing video on Brand’s channel since 18 May, when he interviewed the New Testament scholar Jeremiah Johnston. Prior to that, the last time Brand surpassed 1m views was on 5 December last year, when he published a video conversation he had with the American conservative influencer Candace Owens. Many of his videos in the past year have drawn only between 50,000 and 100,000 views.

output.headline: McFadden's daughter speaks out and considers legal action over Cooper plagiarism claims
output.bodyHtml:
Caroline McFadden, the daughter of the novelist Cyra McFadden, says she is considering legal action after Jilly Cooper, the bestselling Rivals author who died last year, was accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists.

She told the Observer: “To steal her work so extensively and to profit off it is unconscionable.”

“It absolutely boils my blood to think of someone stealing my mother’s work because I know how hard she worked at her craft,” she said.

“I will be looking at legal options as this can’t be allowed to stand. I sincerely hope that all of Dame Cooper’s work will be scrutinised to see if this was a pattern of hers and other talented authors’ work stolen.”

The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey.

According to a report in the Observer, Cooper, who died last October, committed “what appears to be extensive and deliberate plagiarism” by lifting at least 35 passages from The Serial alone.

Cooper, who has sold more than 11m copies of her books in the UK alone, was given a damehood in the 2024 new year honours list for her services to literature and charity.

Disney+ is currently airing the second series of Rivals, the award-winning television adaptation of her most famous work. The show combines TV industry intrigue and racy sex scenes against the backdrop of the Cotswolds countryside in the fictional guise of Rutshire.

In its investigation, the Observer detailed 15 allegedly plagiarised passages from The Serial, which was first published from late 1975 as a weekly serialisation in a US newspaper before it was released as a book in May 1977.

In The Serial, McFadden, who died in 2024, created the off-and-on-again couple Kate and Harvey Holroyd, two progressives in California’s Marin County. The Observer noted several similarities with the dialogue in Cooper’s character, Berenice, an American feminist.

In The Serial, Kate says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open, loving relationship, based on growth and trust and sharing, and Harvey wanted his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we just weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

In Prudence, Berenice says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open living relationship based on trust and growth, and all he wanted was his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

The publication also cited another example from The Serial in which Harvey was offered lifestyle advice. The passage said: “Cut out the nine-to-five shit, Harv. You gotta get in touch with the universe. That’s the first step.”

In Prudence, Berenice offered similar advice. “You ought to cut out that nine to five shit … And get in touch with the universe.”

The Observer said it began looking at Prudence after a reader pointed out similarities with a scene in Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair.

The publication alleged that Cooper “lifts directly” from chapter 22 of the novel “both in narrative architecture and in line-by-line choice of words”. Tey died in 1952 and left no heirs.

Cooper is said to have praised The Serial for its parody of the modern feminist in a 1982 Mail on Sunday column. She said she was “tremendously comforted” when she “came across a passage in the novel The Serial by Cyra McFadden, a marvellously funny send-up of American trendies in the late seventies”.

An inquest held last year concluded that Cooper suffered a fatal head injury in a fall at her Gloucestershire home. She was found by family on 4 October 2025 and died in hospital the following day.

The Guardian has contacted Cooper’s agent, Felicity Blunt at Curtis Brown, and her publisher, Penguin, for comment. The Observer said both had declined to provide a comment.
output.standfirst: Caroline McFadden says she may take legal action after an Observer investigation found extensive similarities between Jilly Cooper's 1978 novel Prudence and her mother Cyra McFadden's The Serial, and Josephine Tey's The Franchise Affair.
output.progress: Caroline McFadden is considering legal action and wants Cooper's other books scrutinised for similar borrowing.
